title: Passover: the seder plate
hookLine: bitter herbs, charoset, shank bone, egg, greens and salt water each speak

lines: A BONE, AN EGG, A BITTER ROOT.
cards: At the center of the seder table sits a plate that makes no sense as dinner. A roasted bone with almost no meat on it. A hard-boiled egg, often scorched.
A pile of horseradish so sharp it makes grown adults cry. A sweet brown paste of apples and nuts. A sprig of parsley, or a slice of potato.
Nearby, a bowl of salt water. Nobody eats most of it as a meal. It's there so that, at the right moment, someone can point at each thing and say what it means.

teach.b: Start with the bitter herbs, maror. Of the Passover lamb, the Torah says, in the old Jewish translation: "with bitter herbs they shall eat it."
The bitterness is the taste of slavery: the Egyptians, the Haggadah says, made the Israelites' lives bitter. Some use horseradish; others use romaine lettuce, which turns bitter as it grows.
A second bitter herb, chazeret, sits beside it for the sandwich later in the night.
Next, charoset, the sweet paste. The Talmud says it recalls the mortar the slaves used for bricks. So the sweetest thing on the plate is a memory of forced labor.
Then the shank bone, zeroa. It recalls the lamb offered on the night of the Exodus, and its name means arm, the outstretched arm the Torah says brought Israel out. It's not eaten.
The Talmud even mentions using a beet instead, and some vegetarians still do.
The roasted egg, beitzah, recalls the festival offering brought in Temple times; some also see mourning in it, since eggs are eaten by mourners.
Then karpas, a green vegetable, dipped in salt water early in the seder. The green is spring. The salt water, some say, is tears.
Families arrange the plate in different ways, following different teachers.
The mystic Isaac Luria laid it out in a pattern of two triangles, and families who follow him set it that way; others simply line the items up. Under the differences sits one idea.
The plate is a set of props for telling a story, so that the story isn't only heard. It's tasted.

how: At the Passover seder, a plate holds maror, chazeret, charoset, the zeroa, a roasted egg and karpas, with salt water beside it; during the Haggadah the leader points to them and explains, and some items are eaten at set points.

o: the feast of booths after the autumn harvest
the festival of leaving Egypt, told at the seder
the night the Torah was given at Mount Sinai

games.q: on the seder plate — tap the pairs.

s: the shank bone on the seder plate is eaten at the meal

games.q: you're setting the seder plate and want something to recall the mortar the slaves used for bricks. what do you add?
o: the sweet paste of apples and nuts.
games.why: charoset: the sweetest thing on the plate is the memory of forced labor.

practice: Find one object near you that carries a story, a ring, a mug, a photo, a key, and rest your eyes on it. Ask it, quietly, what it remembers: who gave it, or what it got you through.
Then say its meaning to yourself in one sentence, the way someone points to the bone on the plate and explains it.

wordCard.voice: Passover. The festival of leaving Egypt, and the seder plate, where bitter herbs, charoset, bone, egg, greens and salt water each tell part of it. Today's word.
